title: How can a fold split a straight angle into two equal angles?
description: Three points A, O and B are marked in a line along the edge of a rectangular paper, which makes a straight angle. The paper is folded so that OB lands on OA, and the crease through O is the line that splits the angle. Keeko's doubt is that folding the paper in half anywhere gives the line.
teaching_notes: One idea: fold one arm onto the other, and the crease through the vertex splits the straight angle into two equal angles. Watch for students who fold anywhere and expect the crease to pass through the vertex.

maths_rules: A, O and B lie in a line along one edge with O between them: the straight angle AOB
fold the paper so that OB lies exactly on OA
the crease through O is the line OC
the crease splits the straight angle into two equal angles
slip: a fold elsewhere may miss O or leave the two angles unequal

<bookmark mark='edge'/>Mark three points eigh, oh and bee along one edge, with oh in the middle. Two arms in one line make what is called a straight angle.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Fold the paper to get a line through oh. The line should cut the angle into two equal angles. How can it be done?

<bookmark mark='line'/>This line is always straight, and it is called a crease.
